Lycaonia
lik-ā-ō'ni-ä
n. (an inland district of Asia Minor containing Lystra and Derbe, where Paul was taken for a god and then stoned)
From Greek Lukaonia, the inland plain of southern Asia Minor. Luke notes that its people kept their own tongue — “the speech of Lycaonia” — distinct from the Greek in which Paul had just spoken.

Biblical Definition

Lycaonia is the district of Lystra and Derbe, and it stages one of the most instructive scenes in Acts. Driven from Iconium, “they fled unto Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and unto the region that lieth round about” (Act 14:6). There Paul healed a man crippled from birth, and the crowd drew the conclusion their own religion supplied: “when the people saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in the speech of Lycaonia, The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men” (Act 14:11). They called Barnabas Jupiter and Paul Mercurius and brought oxen and garlands to the gates. The apostles tore their clothes and ran in among them, and what they preached to raw pagans is worth marking — not the covenants, but creation and providence: turn from these vanities to the living God, who made heaven and earth and gave you rain and fruitful seasons (Act 14:15-17). Within days the same crowd, worked on by hostile Jews from Antioch and Iconium, stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city for dead (Act 14:19). Adoration and murder from one crowd in one week. And out of Lycaonia came Timothy (Act 16:1), so the province that nearly killed Paul gave him his dearest son in the faith.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Lycaonia; it is an inland district of Asia Minor whose cities were Lystra, Derbe and Iconium, and whose people had their own speech.

expand to see more

LYCAONIA, n. An inland region of Asia Minor, bordering upon Cappadocia, Galatia, Phrygia, Pisidia and Cilicia.

Its principal cities named in the Acts are Lystra and Derbe.

The inhabitants retained a native tongue, called the speech of Lycaonia.

There Paul and Barnabas were taken for Mercurius and Jupiter, and sacrifice was prepared to them.

There also Paul was stoned and drawn out of the city, and there Timothy was found.

Key Scripture

Act 14:6 — "They were ware of it, and fled unto Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and unto the region that lieth round about:"

Act 14:11 — "And when the people saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in the speech of Lycaonia, The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men."

Act 14:15 — "And saying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein:"

Act 14:19 — "And there came thither certain Jews from Antioch and Iconium, who persuaded the people, and, having stoned Paul, drew him out of the city, supposing he had been dead."

Modern Corruption

The refusal of worship at Lystra is treated as ancient modesty rather than as doctrine, while the same instinct that deified two travellers is alive wherever a preacher is exalted above his message.

expand to see more

Paul and Barnabas ran in among the crowd tearing their clothes, and the reason they gave was doctrinal, not modest: “We also are men of like passions with you”. That sentence is the whole of the biblical doctrine of the minister. He is not a mediator, not a channel of grace in himself, not a man of a different order; there is “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5). The dictionary names as corruption every system that reverses this — the veneration of saints, the priest who stands between, the modern celebrity ministry with its untouchable platform. The Lycaonian error is not extinct; it has changed its vocabulary. And it is a fearful thing that men who accepted such honour in Acts came to bad ends: Herod took the shout “It is the voice of a god, and not of a man” and was eaten of worms (Act 12:22-23).

The second thing to notice is the sermon. To a pagan crowd with no Scripture, Paul does not begin with Moses; he begins with the Creator, the rain, the fruitful seasons, and the witness God has left of Himself in every man's food and gladness. Modern evangelism often assumes a hearer who already grants the categories — sin, judgment, a personal God — and is confused when he does not. Paul assumed nothing and started at Genesis 1. Where a culture has forgotten that it is made, the first work of preaching is not comfort but creation: “In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth” (Gen 1:1).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek Lukaonia (G3071), Lycaonia; Lukaonisti (G3072), in the speech of Lycaonia; homoiopathes (G3663), of like passions; mataios (G3152), vain, empty; lithazo (G3034), to stone.

expand to see more

Greek Lukaonia (G3071) — Lycaonia; the inland district of Lystra and Derbe.

Greek Lukaonisti (G3072) — in the Lycaonian tongue; Luke's note that the crowd spoke its own speech.

Greek homoiopathes (G3663) — of like passions, of the same nature; the apostles' refusal of worship.

Greek mataios (G3152) — vain, empty, futile; “these vanities” from which they were to turn.

Greek lithazo (G3034) — to stone; what the same crowd did to Paul within days.

Usage

"“The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men” — paganism's reflex before a miracle."

"“We also are men of like passions with you” — the whole doctrine of the ministry in nine words."

"“Having stoned Paul, drew him out of the city” — the same crowd, the same week."
